title: High oil prices raise prospect of accelerated EV sales | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Ed Crooks argues the Gulf conflict — Brent above US$108, US diesel at a record US$5.98/gallon and NY ULSD above the equivalent of US$200/bbl — could break the long-standing rule that EV sales are insensitive to fuel prices, because low-priced Chinese EVs have finally made the fuel-cost argument decisive. Wood Mackenzie's 'Electric Shock' Horizons scenario sketches a 2040 global EV fleet ~50% above base case, constrained by lithium (+14%) far more than copper (+2% of supply), with structurally lower long-term oil demand as the lasting consequence of the Iran war.

insights.claim: The conventional wisdom that EV sales are not driven by fuel prices is breaking down, because a wave of low-priced Chinese EVs plus mid-market models from Tesla, Volkswagen and Hyundai changes the purchase equation from status and environment to running cost.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: If EV demand becomes fuel-price elastic, oil price spikes now destroy future demand permanently rather than temporarily — a structural repricing of long-dated oil.
insights.quote: Conventional wisdom until now has been that EV sales have generally not been driven by fuel prices.
insights.locator: Conventional wisdom until now has been

insights.claim: Prolonged disruption to Gulf crude and product flows has raised the prospect that worldwide EV adoption progresses significantly faster than looked likely at the start of 2026.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Geopolitical oil risk is now a demand-destruction mechanism, not just a price event — the longer the disruption, the worse the terminal value of oil assets.
insights.locator: After the rise in fuel prices that followed

insights.claim: The third and decisive condition for accelerated EV adoption is consumers concluding that high and volatile fuel prices are permanent, cementing the economics of EV ownership.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Watch consumer inflation-expectation and fuel-price-expectation surveys as a leading indicator for EV order books — sentiment, not the spot price, is the trigger.
insights.quote: Consumers need to decide that high and volatile fuel prices are here to stay, cementing the economic benefits of EV ownership.
insights.locator: To get to that future of accelerated EV adoption

insights.claim: Progress is already visible on two of the three conditions for faster EV adoption, with BYD, Geely and CATL announcing remarkable advances in fast charging in China.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Chinese battery and OEM champions are removing the charging-time objection — the main remaining non-price barrier to mass EV adoption.
insights.locator: There are already signs of progress on 1) and 2)

insights.claim: Brent crude rose above US$108 a barrel following strikes on oil tankers by both Iran and the US and Houthi gains on Yemen's Red Sea coast, its highest since May.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Tanker strikes, not production outages, are now the marginal price driver — shipping and insurance channels are where the next escalation shows up first.
insights.locator: The latest escalation in the conflict

insights.claim: Ultra-low sulphur diesel in New York harbour has been trading at the equivalent of more than US$200 a barrel, with Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries compounding global product-market tightness.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Refining margins, not crude, are where the extreme value sits — the crack spread is the cleaner expression of this conflict than flat price.
insights.quote: Ultra-low sulphur diesel in New York harbour has been trading this week at the equivalent of more than US$200 a barrel.
insights.locator: The impact on fuel prices from the conflict

insights.claim: US retail diesel has been hitting new all-time highs at about US$5.98 a gallon, even while gasoline at US$4.28 a gallon remains well below its June 2022 record of about US$5.02.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The pain is concentrated in freight and agriculture rather than the consumer pump price — a distinct inflation transmission channel from 2022.
insights.locator: The average retail price of gasoline in the US

insights.claim: US retail gasoline at about US$4.28 a gallon is up roughly 34% year-over-year, a large enough move to shift consumer vehicle purchase economics.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A 34% fuel-cost jump is the size of shock that historically moves vehicle mix — watch US EV share data for the first sign the elasticity thesis is real.
insights.locator: The average retail price of gasoline in the US

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia's August oil production fell to 6.238 million b/d, its lowest since 1990 and down about 1.9 million b/d from July, but market supply held at 7.122 million b/d because barrels were released from storage.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Saudi is masking a production collapse with inventory draws — when storage is exhausted, the ~800 kb/d gap hits the market and prices gap higher.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia’s oil production last month dropped

insights.claim: President Trump said he expected the Gulf war to end immediately after the 3 November US midterm elections, while the Wall Street Journal reported his advisers had raised the possibility it drags on through the remainder of his term to January 2029.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The gap between the political promise and the advisers' scenario is the entire oil risk premium — a multi-year disruption is not priced by the consensus.
insights.locator: President Donald Trump said on Wednesday

insights.claim: Accelerated EV growth and structurally lower long-term oil demand could prove to be one of the lasting consequences of the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The strategic risk for oil producers is that a war which raises near-term prices permanently lowers terminal demand — a classic self-defeating rally.
insights.quote: Accelerated growth in EVs, and structurally lower long-term oil demand, could turn out to be one of the lasting consequences of the Iran war.
insights.locator: Accelerated growth in EVs

insights.claim: Over January to July 2026, BEV sales were up 69% year-over-year in France, 51% in Germany and 29% in the UK.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: European BEV growth is already running far ahead of trend — European gasoline demand forecasts are likely too high.
insights.locator: EV sales have surged in several markets

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie estimates BEVs will be about 30% of light passenger vehicle sales in Thailand this year and almost 25% in South Korea.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Emerging Asia is adopting EVs faster than the US, undercutting the assumption that EV penetration tracks income levels.
insights.locator: Some Asian markets have also been very strong

insights.claim: BEVs are expected to account for about 40% of Chinese vehicle sales this year even though China's overall car market has been weak.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: EV share gains in China are coming from ICE cannibalisation in a shrinking market, which means Chinese gasoline demand is falling outright.
insights.locator: In China the car market has been weak

insights.claim: BEVs are expected to be only about 6% of US car sales this year, making the US an outlier among major vehicle markets for its slow EV adoption.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A 6% base gives the US the most room for an upside surprise if fuel prices stay high — asymmetric versus already-saturated European markets.
insights.locator: The US is an outlier among major vehicle markets

themes.theme: China export machine vs US retreat

insights.claim: China sold more vehicles abroad in the first eight months of 2026 than in the whole of 2025, with about half of those export sales being new energy vehicles.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: China is converting the global EV boom into export share at record pace — a direct share loss for European, Japanese and Korean OEMs in third markets.
insights.locator: China has been one of the principal beneficiaries

insights.claim: Ford has discontinued the F-150 Lightning electric truck that was seen as critical to US electrification and is instead trying again with a low-cost EV platform.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The US OEM pivot from halo trucks to low-cost platforms validates Christensen's disruption path — watch Ford's cost-per-kWh targets, not its EV volume guidance.
insights.locator: US vehicle manufacturers have abandoned plans

insights.claim: General Motors CEO Mary Barra describes EVs as the company's 'end game' rather than an imminent transformation, signalling a deliberately slow transition.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: GM is optioning rather than committing to EVs, which protects near-term margins but raises the risk of being late if fuel prices force the shift.
insights.quote: its CEO Mary Barra describes EVs as the “end game” for the company, not an imminent transformation
insights.locator: General Motors is still moving towards electrification

insights.claim: US manufacturers are shielded at home by tariff rates above 125% on imported Chinese EVs plus restrictions on Chinese electronic hardware, software and connectivity, but face share loss internationally where those barriers do not exist.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Protection at home is not protection abroad — Detroit's international franchises are the exposed asset, and a hidden earnings risk.
insights.quote: In their home market, US manufacturers are protected by tariff rates of more than 125% on imported Chinese EVs
insights.locator: In their home market, US manufacturers are protected

insights.claim: US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said a BYD-made Chinese EV was 'the best $70,000 car that $35,000 can buy', and while Chinese makers do benefit from tax breaks, grants, low-cost financing and trade-in subsidies, his calculation probably overstates the subsidy-driven cost advantage.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: If the Chinese cost edge is genuine manufacturing capability rather than subsidy, tariffs buy time but do not fix Western OEM competitiveness.
insights.quote: the best $70,000 car that $35,000 can buy
insights.locator: The Trump administration has argued

insights.claim: For a neutral consumer seeking the best available deal, a Chinese EV is simply a great buy regardless of the subsidy debate.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Consumer-level value proposition is what drives share in unprotected markets — expect Chinese OEM share gains wherever tariffs are absent.
insights.locator: But for a neutral consumer who only wants

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Horizons report 'Electric Shock: how electric vehicles could hit the accelerator' maps a scenario where the global EV fleet in 2040 is about 50% larger than the base case.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A published +50% upside scenario from a mainstream forecaster gives an anchor for stress-testing oil demand and battery-metal demand models.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie analysts last month published a report

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's base case projects 2035 passenger EV market share of about 80% in China, about 70% in Europe and almost 30% in the US.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Even the base case implies near-total EV transition in China and Europe by 2035 — ICE component supply chains in those regions are terminal-value impaired.
insights.locator: In our base case, we are forecasting strong growth

insights.claim: Putting 50% more EVs on the roads by 2040 would need another 800,000 tons of copper that year, only about 2% of projected worldwide supply, so copper is not a binding constraint on faster EV adoption.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Undercuts the popular 'copper shortage blocks electrification' narrative — the EV-driven copper bull case is smaller than marketed.
insights.quote: Putting 50% more EVs on the roads by 2040 would require another 800,000 tons of copper supply that year, but that is only about 2% of projected worldwide supply for that year.
insights.locator: Neither metals supply nor grid and charging infrastructure

insights.claim: The accelerated EV scenario would lift 2040 lithium demand by about 14%, a far larger relative impact than copper, and China's dominance of lithium processing and the battery supply chain is the real western vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Lithium, not copper, is the leveraged commodity to an EV upside surprise — and ex-China processing capacity is the scarce strategic asset.
insights.locator: The impact on lithium demand would be greater

insights.claim: Grid problems from EV charging growth are real but manageable if charging is time-shifted to periods when the grid is amply supplied, avoiding the need for massive additional infrastructure investment.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Value accrues to managed-charging software and demand-response platforms rather than to brute-force grid capex.
insights.locator: Similarly, the problems created for the power grid

insights.claim: Governments investing in EV and battery supply chains to reduce reliance on China is the first of three conditions Wood Mackenzie identifies for an accelerated global EV transition.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Policy support for ex-China battery capacity is a precondition, not a nice-to-have — track subsidy programmes as the gating variable for the upside scenario.
insights.locator: To get to that future of accelerated EV adoption

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's base case forecast has world oil demand hitting a plateau in the early 2030s, before any accelerated-EV overlay.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: An early-2030s plateau in the base case means the accelerated scenario implies outright decline — reserve-replacement-heavy oil business models are the ones at risk.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie’s base case forecast shows world oil demand

insights.claim: Clayton Christensen's 'The Innovator's Dilemma' predicted 30 years ago that EVs would need to be simple, reliable, convenient, rapidly evolving and cheaper than gasoline rivals — a description that now fits the Chinese EV industry rather than Western incumbents.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Framing Chinese EVs as the classic low-end disruptor implies incumbent share loss is structural, not cyclical, and accelerates once the product is 'good enough'.
insights.locator: Clayton Christensen’s ‘The Innovators’ Dilemma’

insights.claim: Christensen specifically warned about the dangers of aiming EVs at unnecessarily high performance and about obstruction from established dealer networks, both of which materialised.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Explains why premium-first EV strategies (and the discontinued F-150 Lightning) failed — screen OEM EV strategies for the low-end entry path instead.
insights.locator: Writing 30 years ago, Christensen predicted

insights.claim: The oil price surge stoked inflation fears that drove the 10-year US Treasury yield above 4.96%, its highest since 2023, and the 30-year to about 5.37%, the highest since 2007.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A 30-year at 2007 highs raises the cost of capital for exactly the long-duration energy projects the transition needs — a direct headwind to renewables IRRs.
insights.locator: Bond prices have been tumbling

insights.claim: Trump's pledge to pay US$5,000 to every US citizen if Republicans retain Congress at the midterms is adding to inflation concerns alongside the oil price.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A fiscal-plus-energy inflation shock going into the midterms is a bearish combination for the long end — position for curve steepening risk around 3 November.
insights.locator: As well as oil prices, other factors

insights.claim: Higher interest rates are raising the cost of capital for households and businesses but have not yet produced a general expectation of downturn; Wood Mackenzie forecast in July that US GDP grows about 1.9% in 2026, an upgrade from 1.7%.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Growth forecasts are still being revised up despite the oil and rate shock — the recession trade is early until those revisions turn.
insights.locator: The higher interest rates will raise the cost of capital

insights.claim: Google plans to invest about US$15 billion in Finland for data centres and supporting electricity infrastructure, and has signed a 22-year power purchase agreement supporting a life extension of a nearby nuclear plant plus an MoU with Fortum on possible new nuclear generation.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A 22-year hyperscaler PPA funding nuclear life extension is the template for how AI capex underwrites existing nuclear — watch for replication at other utilities.
insights.locator: Google plans to invest about US$15 billion in Finland

insights.claim: Finland's government support for data centre investment combined with a subarctic climate that cuts cooling energy costs is making the country a preferred hyperscaler location.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Cold-climate, policy-friendly Nordic locations are winning marginal data centre siting decisions — relevant to Nordic power demand and utility offtake.
insights.locator: Finland’s government supports data centre investment

insights.claim: Diamondback Energy chief executive Kaes Van't Hof says oil has flipped from a dying industry to a respectable, well-paying career sitting at the intersection of AI and energy, while 'the tech guys' are now seen as the villains.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A talent-flow and sentiment reversal toward oil and gas is a contrarian marker — narrative rehabilitation typically precedes multiple expansion in energy equities.
insights.quote: A few years back every other day there was an article about how oil is dead, right? But now I think people realise that this is a respectable industry that pays well and is well placed at the intersection of AI and energy
insights.locator: Quote of the week
